description:
We are the chicken Invaders team. We're students at grade 10 who are interested in space, physics,  programming and content creation. 

We're web developers, Ai programmers and students in different levels in DECI.
summary: "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars." Since the 1960s, NASA has left hardware across the solar system–on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. From rovers and instruments that completed their science missions to probes still traveling away from Earth this hardware varies widely in both its purpose and current level of functionality. Our challenge is to tell the story of some or all of this equipment that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to the hardware and the science it made possible. we decided to make an interactive website to be accessible for everyone, but when you connect this website to a VR and the hardware needed it makes you live the experience of an astronaut traveling through space. You're in a room wearing the VR experiencing the whole journey of an astronaut from the launching of the spaceship until landing on the moon or wherever you want in this large space, learning about those abundant tools by hearing from the inventors of these tools. This can be provided in schools, universities and more learning places to help them experience more than a website talking about these hardware.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Our project is an interactive, web-based educational experience designed to bring forgotten space hardware back to life. Instead of dry historical textbooks, users navigate an immersive digital platform where they can explore iconic off-world artifacts left behind by NASA—specifically focusing on the Apollo 15 Lunar Module ("Falcon") on the Moon and the Pioneer 10 spacecraft in deep space. By clicking on interactive hotspots on 3D models or blueprints of the hardware, users unlock detailed structural breakdowns, scientific payloads, and narrative "ghost transmissions" or stories that explain how these machines operated.

What benefits does it have?

The platform bridges the gap between complex NASA archival data and casual learners, particularly school-age space enthusiasts. It transforms dense technical specifications (such as spacecraft telemetry, nuclear power sources, and orbital mechanics) into an accessible, engaging, and visually intuitive format that promotes self-paced learning and curiosity about space exploration.

What is intended impact of the project?

The primary goal is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and space explorers. By highlighting the untold stories and groundbreaking science behind historical space missions—rather than focusing solely on active ones—we foster a personal emotional connection between the audience and humanity's robotic pioneers resting across the solar system.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Data Sources & APIs: Official NASA historical mission logs, NSSDC archives, and technical specifications (e.g., Apollo 15 and Pioneer 10 mission profiles).
  • Development & Content Architecture: Structured technical breakdowns (Component -> Function -> Contribution to Mission Success) for front-end implementation.
  • Design & Multimedia Assets: Interactive blueprints, structural component mapping (Ascent/Descent stages, RTG nuclear power generators, ALSEP stations, and the Pioneer Plaque), and narrative scripts tailored for web integration.

    How is your project creative?

Our project breaks away from traditional static articles by blending hard science with immersive storytelling. We personify or contextualize the hardware through narrative logs and structural blueprints, turning mechanical components (like landing probes, MESA racks, and high-gain antennas) into interactive story elements. This gamified, exploration-driven approach makes learning about space hardware feel like an active archaeological dig in space.


What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific Accuracy: Every piece of hardware data, coordinate, and technical specification (such as SNAP-27 and SNAP-19 nuclear RTGs, or spacecraft mass and trajectories) was strictly derived from official NASA records.
  • Target Audience Accessibility: We tailored the language and UI concept to be captivating and easy to digest for young space enthusiasts without losing technical depth.
  • Resource Optimization (Best Use of Data): We focused heavily on how to translate raw historical and scientific data into a meaningful, functional web application architecture.
